name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Thursday 15 August 1974

clue.text: Means hail-storms

blocks.note: Ave is the Latin greeting, a hail
to storm is to rage

explanation.surface: A weather report: what hailstorms mean, or a forecaster's terse note.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen glues hail to storms, but the two words give separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: In statistics a mean is an average, so means are averages.

clue.text: Liqueur for the Oakley clique (zo they zay)

indicators.note: mock West Country speech for 'so they say', marking a spoken version in a rural accent

blocks.note: Annie Oakley was the American sharpshooter; her clique is her set

explanation.surface: A drink served to the Oakley crowd, as country gossip has it.
explanation.walkthrough: Annie Oakley was the Wild West sharpshooter; her circle, said in a stage yokel's voice, gives the drink's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Anisette is a sweet aniseed-flavoured liqueur from France.

clue.text: In the end the turbulent Rhine's held sacred

indicators.note: turbulent water churns, so the river's letters are churned into a new order
In places the following word inside the other one

blocks.note: taken as written
the river's name with its possessive s

explanation.surface: In the end the swirling Rhine's waters were revered, like a holy river.
explanation.walkthrough: In the end reads as 'finally'; In is the insertion signal and the end is the outer word.
explanation.definitionFit: To enshrine something is to cherish it as sacred, as relics are kept in a shrine.

clue.text: Metric unit like the things it measures

blocks.note: an are is a metric unit of land, 100 square metres
as means like

explanation.surface: A puzzle about a metric unit that resembles what it measures.
explanation.walkthrough: The are measures surfaces, so the definition neatly circles back to the first piece.
explanation.definitionFit: An are is a unit of surface, so areas are precisely what it is used to measure.

clue.text: An interchange to get on transport

indicators.note: to change something is to alter it, so the letters before it are reordered

blocks.note: An plus the first half of interchange, inter, are the letters to rearrange; the second half is the signal

explanation.surface: A road junction where travellers switch to the bus or train.
explanation.walkthrough: Interchange must be split in two: inter is fodder, change the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To entrain is to board a train, a transport sense used especially of troops.

clue.text: Returning ships may hold fishing lines?

indicators.note: something returning goes back the way it came, so the word is read from its end

blocks.note: sloops are small sailing ships

explanation.surface: Fishing boats coming home with their lines on board.
explanation.definitionFit: Reels or bobbins wound with fishing line are spools; the question mark admits the definition is by example.

clue.text: Copy pictures — almost an art gallery

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the gallery's name loses its last letter

blocks.note: photos are pictures
the Tate is the London art gallery

explanation.surface: Reproducing paintings to fill what is nearly a whole gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tate is the national gallery of British art in London.
explanation.definitionFit: A Photostat was a photographic duplicate, and the trade name became a verb meaning to make a copy.

clue.text: Beast of a pig— no tail, but all right in the head

indicators.note: an animal with no tail lacks its end, so the final letter goes

blocks.note: OK means all right; in the head puts it first
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tailless pig of an animal that is at least sane.
explanation.walkthrough: All right in the head sounds like sanity; it places the agreement word at the head.
explanation.definitionFit: The okapi is an African forest animal related to the giraffe, a beast in the zoological sense.

clue.text: Countrymen are .vegetables

blocks.note: first meaning: natives of a particular country, Sweden
second meaning: yellow root vegetables, rutabagas

explanation.surface: A sneer that rural folk are dull as turnips.
explanation.walkthrough: Countrymen suggests rustics; it means people of one country. A swede is the British name for a rutabaga.
explanation.definitionFit: Natives of Sweden are Swedes, and the swede is the root crop Americans call rutabaga.

clue.text: This missile makes a terrible crater

indicators.note: something terrible is a wreck of itself, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: the six letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A warning that a certain shell blasts an awful hole.
explanation.definitionFit: A tracer is a bullet or shell that leaves a glowing trail so its flight can be followed.

clue.text: Playful caller

blocks.note: surface reading: a frisky visitor who drops round in high spirits
setter's reading: belonging to a play

explanation.walkthrough: Playful is read as 'from a play': in J. B. Priestley's An Inspector Calls the title character is the one who calls.
explanation.definitionFit: The police officer who calls on the Birling family in Priestley's drama is the play's title figure.

clue.text: Egg-shaped vessel in Old English

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits inside it, so the vessel goes within the abbreviation

blocks.note: OE is the standard abbreviation for Old English
a vat is a large vessel for liquids

explanation.surface: An oval pot found among Old English artefacts.
explanation.definitionFit: Ovate is the botanist's word for oval with one end broader, the outline of an egg.

clue.text: Note a senior service's merits

blocks.note: E is a musical note
taken as written
the Royal Navy, Britain's oldest armed service, is called the senior service
the possessive ending supplies its letter

explanation.surface: A memo recording what a naval officer's service deserves.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Navy is nicknamed the senior service because it is the oldest of Britain's forces.
explanation.definitionFit: To merit a reward is to deserve it, which is what one earns.

clue.text: A recluse has-to fix it with a rope's end

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: to anchor something is to fix it in place
taken as written
the last letter of rope

explanation.surface: A hermit who must tie something down with the tail of a rope.
explanation.walkthrough: The odd hyphen in has-to is a period typesetting quirk; read it as 'has to'.
explanation.definitionFit: An anchorite is a religious hermit who withdraws from the world, the classic recluse.

clue.text: Ten to one on rounding the point — what a strain!

indicators.note: to round something is to go about it, so the odds wrap around the point

blocks.note: taken as written
I is the Roman numeral one
taken as written
S, south, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A bettor at odds-on watching the race go round the final bend, nerves fraying.
explanation.walkthrough: Ten to one on is betting odds, but here 'to' just joins the pieces; the point sits between ten and one-on: TEN-S-ION.
explanation.definitionFit: Strain and tension are synonyms for pull or stress, whether on a rope or the nerves.

clue.text: A form of flattery that's somewhat spurious

blocks.note: first meaning: copying, the sincerest form of flattery in the proverb
second meaning: fake, not genuine, as an adjective

explanation.surface: A remark that one kind of compliment is a bit insincere.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb says imitation is the sincerest form of flattery.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun it is copying; used before another noun, as in imitation leather, it means fake.

clue.text: Confirm there's a proper setback when Ray's out

indicators.note: a setback here is a thing set backwards, so the word runs right to left
Ray being out means the name stands outside, enclosing the rest

blocks.note: taken as written
fit means suitable or proper

explanation.surface: Someone confirms a team suffered a real blow with Ray sidelined.
explanation.walkthrough: Ray's out reads like a player injured or dropped; it means the name goes around the reversed pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To ratify a treaty or decision is to confirm it formally.

clue.text: Sadly so often a journalist gets decorated

indicators.note: sadly means in a sorry state, so the words are knocked out of order

blocks.note: the seven letters to be rearranged
ED, editor, is the usual crossword journalist

explanation.surface: A lament that newspaper writers keep receiving honours.
explanation.walkthrough: Decorated suggests medals for the journalist; it means adorned.
explanation.definitionFit: Festooned means hung with garlands or chains of ornament, thoroughly decorated.

clue.text: Fabulously made-up!

blocks.note: surface reading: wearing wonderful cosmetics
setter's reading: invented in the manner of a fable or legend

explanation.walkthrough: Fabulous and made-up sound like a compliment on someone's make-up; read literally, they mean belonging to fable and invented.
explanation.definitionFit: Something mythical exists only in myth or fable, an invented story rather than fact.

clue.text: A pile of snow like an icefloe?

blocks.note: taken as written
wind piles snow into a drift

explanation.surface: A polar scene: a snowbank and a floating slab of ice.
explanation.definitionFit: An ice floe floats loose on the sea, unmoored, which is what being adrift means.

clue.text: Flute part, played -by following this

indicators.note: only part of the ornament is wanted, so its last letter is dropped

blocks.note: a trill is a rapid ornament characteristic of the flute
taken as written, the hyphen an OCR or print artefact

explanation.surface: A flautist's part, performed by reading this sheet.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is oblique: this, the thing played, is Trilby, du Maurier's novel whose 1895 stage version was a famous hit; the wordplay is part of a trill followed by by.
explanation.definitionFit: Trilby was George du Maurier's 1894 novel, adapted into a celebrated play, so it was something played.

clue.text: It is poetic and loud in, say, content

indicators.note: the phrase sits in the other word, so it is placed inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
'tis is the poetic contraction of it is
f, forte, is the musical mark for loud

explanation.surface: A critic notes that a work is poetic and loud in its content.
explanation.walkthrough: Content looks like a noun, the matter of a poem; it is the verb, to please.
explanation.definitionFit: To content someone is to give them what they want, which is to satisfy them.

clue.text: That is seen in kinds of operational flights

indicators.note: seen in places the first phrase inside the word for kinds

blocks.note: sorts are kinds
i.e. is the Latin abbreviation id est, that is

explanation.surface: A note that a certain feature appears in various types of military flying.
explanation.definitionFit: A sortie is a single operational mission flown by a military aircraft.

clue.text: Silver instrument in harmony

blocks.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
a reed is a wind instrument, or a pipe of one

explanation.surface: A silver flute or oboe playing in tune with the band.
explanation.walkthrough: In harmony looks musical alongside the instrument; it means of one mind.
explanation.definitionFit: People who have agreed are in accord, of the same opinion.

clue.text: Alexander's better musically if British

blocks.note: surface reading: someone who outdoes Alexander the Great, or a gambler on him
setter's reading: an old regimental marching song that ranks a British infantryman above Alexander

explanation.walkthrough: The marching song begins 'Some talk of Alexander, and some of Hercules' and ends that none can compare with the British soldier of its title.
explanation.definitionFit: The regimental march The British Grenadiers names this infantryman as the hero who surpasses Alexander.

clue.text: He gets the bird -about lunch-time

indicators.note: about means around, so the bird wraps around the time

blocks.note: the erne is the sea eagle, a crossword favourite
one o'clock is lunch-time, and I is the Roman one

explanation.surface: A comedian booed off stage at midday.
explanation.walkthrough: Getting the bird means being jeered, but here it is the sea eagle. He stands for a man's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Ernie is a man's name, so the pronoun stands in for him.

clue.text: General stall

blocks.note: first meaning: William ..., founding General of the Salvation Army
second meaning: a market stand or compartment

explanation.walkthrough: General looks like an adjective; it is a rank, held by the Salvation Army's founder, William Booth.
explanation.definitionFit: Booth was the Salvation Army's first General, and a booth is a small stand at a market or fair.

clue.text: Bloody impetuous and bumptious!

blocks.note: b is the printed euphemism for bloody, as in 'b-- awful'
rash means impetuous

explanation.surface: An exasperated verdict on a cocky, headstrong person.
explanation.walkthrough: Bloody reads as an intensifier; it gives the initial printed for the swearword. Impetuous belongs to the wordplay, not the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Brash and bumptious both describe someone loud and self-assertive to the point of rudeness.

clue.text: One sort of tube in nine perhaps is the result of boring

indicators.note: perhaps signals the word is only one possible arrangement of its letters
the tube is placed in the other word, inside its letters

blocks.note: a U-tube is a sort of tube, named for its letter shape
taken as written

explanation.surface: A drilling engineer reports that a pipe in nine boreholes is what the work turned up.
explanation.walkthrough: Boring suggests drilling holes; it means being tedious.
explanation.definitionFit: Ennui is weary listlessness, exactly the feeling that tedium produces.

clue.text: The majestic style of our monarchs

definitions.text: The majestic style of our monarchs

blocks.note: surface reading: the grand manner in which kings and queens carry themselves
setter's reading: the formal title used for British sovereigns, as in Her ... Majesty

explanation.walkthrough: Style here is the formal title, not manner: British monarchs are styled His or Her Britannic Majesty.
explanation.definitionFit: The official title of the British sovereign in treaties and passports is Her Britannic Majesty.

clue.text: Colourful activity said to be moribund

indicators.note: said means spoken, so what counts is how the word sounds, not its spelling

blocks.note: moribund means at the point of death

explanation.surface: A cheerful pastime, rumoured to be on its last legs.
explanation.definitionFit: Dyeing cloth or hair is the work of putting colour into it.

clue.text: Can processing soda help in this plant?

indicators.note: processing works raw material over into something new, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the eight letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A question about a factory: could treating soda be of use there?
explanation.walkthrough: Plant looks like a factory, as the canning surface suggests; it is a flower.
explanation.definitionFit: The asphodel is a lily-family flower, in legend the bloom of the Elysian fields.
